Class JumpIn

java.lang.Object
dev.swordai.core.rl.JumpIn
public final class JumpIn extends Object
Three jumps that are made for the fighter, and what its keys do in the air of each. Like the rule about answering a hit (AnswerRule) this is not the network's to leave out: the keys it takes are taken from the network for the tick, and what the network learns it learns around them.
  • The chase. It is at a run after an opponent a step or two beyond its reach, and the run is hardly catching it: the opponent is backing off or running. From where the way down of a jump will bring that opponent into reach, it jumps, keeps W and the sprint key down on the way up, and on the way down, once the opponent is in its reach and under its crosshair, lets go of both for a tick and swings on the next: a critical hit, half as much damage again as the sprint hit the run would have come to, and one that leaves the opponent where it is instead of sending it on its way. If the opponent is never in reach it lands still running, and nothing was spent but the jump. After an opponent that runs with its back turned, as fast as the fighter itself, it makes one running jump after the other from any distance: a run never gets nearer to that one, and jumps taken in a row are carried a quarter faster than a run.
  • The crit in its face. Its last two hits did not send the opponent away: each time, by the time the sword was back, the opponent was still on top of it. And now it has landed a hit again and the opponent is in its face three to five ticks later. That is one a hit does not send away, because it takes no knockback, has a wall behind it or keeps pushing in. A sprint hit gets nothing there that a critical hit does not, and a critical hit does half as much damage again. So it jumps as the sword recharges, with W and the sprint key up, and swings on the way down, and goes on like that for as long as the opponent stays. Against an opponent that a sprint hit sends away this never comes up. Nor against one on a slow connection, which stands where it was hit for a quarter to half a second and then goes flying: by the time the sword is back that one is gone, and a jump made at it would have come down on nothing.
  • The uppercut. In a combo of its own, after two hits or more, now and then: a running jump at the opponent as the sword comes back, and the sprint hit made while it is still going up. The jump carries it in faster than a run, so the hit reaches an opponent that is backing out of the combo, and it comes off the rhythm the others came on.

Everything it goes by is what the network itself is shown: the fighter's own body, and how large and where the opponent is on screen. How far away the opponent is, is read off its height on screen.

Why these are rules: a jump that is tried and comes to nothing costs, a jump at random makes a fighter worse, and so in five runs of 0.14.0 the first thing learned about jumping in a fight was not to. Against a person that keeps running out, it ran after them and never caught them.

Not thread-safe; one per fighter.

    • CHASE_TO

      static final float CHASE_TO
      The farthest it jumps at an opponent that keeps its distance from it entirely. A running jump gains little on a run: its first tick covers 0.48 of a block instead of 0.28, and after that the air carries it at 0.29 a tick. By the tick it is coming down with the sprint let go of, that is a quarter of a block more than the run would have made. (The first version of this took it for a whole block, jumped from 3.8 to 4.3 blocks at an opponent backing off, and came down out of reach: one critical hit from 29 such jumps.)

    • PURSUIT_CLOSING_MOST

      static final float PURSUIT_CLOSING_MOST
      Closing by no more than this on an opponent that is going away at a sprint (PURSUIT_SPEED), which is only ever forwards, so with its back turned and nothing it can swing at: about what a string of running jumps gains on a sprint. After that one it jumps from any distance up to PURSUIT_TO, one running jump after the other, which is the only way it gets any nearer; whichever of them brings the opponent into reach ends in the hit. (At one that backs off with its eyes on the fighter it jumps only from where the way down brings it into reach: coming in on the way up, it would be hit out of the air.)
      See Also:

    • PURSUIT_SPEED

      static final float PURSUIT_SPEED

Without this a fighter that was itself slow for a moment took an opponent backing off with its sword ready for one that was running, and jumped at it from anywhere: against a copy of itself that was three jumps a minute, more than half of them hit out of the air, and none of it held back by having been hit before.

    • CHASE_OFF_TICKS

      static final int CHASE_OFF_TICKS
      Hit in the air of a jump made for it, that kind of jump is not made again for this long, thirty seconds: the opponent may be one that hits a fighter out of the air. Hit out of the air a second time, it is one, and that kind of jump is not made at it again for five minutes (OFF_FOR_GOOD_TICKS), from one round to the next against the same opponent (newRound()); after that it finds out again.

      Fifteen seconds and no more at first. Against a copy of itself, which swings at whatever comes into its reach, more than half of these jumps were hit out of the air, again and again in the same fight: about one in four ended in a critical hit.

  • Method Details

    • chaseInCombo

      public void chaseInCombo(boolean on)
      Whether the chase jump is also the next hit of a combo of its own: it has just landed a hit, the opponent is beyond its reach and backing off, and a run would catch it only slowly. Then the jump is made as soon as the way down will bring the opponent into reach, and the hit is a critical one; and from there again. Against a player who backs out of combos with S that is a combo of critical hits, and it is what the players of the first evening of 0.14.0 did to this fighter. False: no jump at an opponent it has hit in the last fifteen ticks, as before.

    • approachHops

      public void approachHops(boolean on)
      Whether it closes on an opponent five blocks off or more with running jumps, one after the other, instead of a run: they carry it a quarter faster, and the last one ends in a critical hit if its way down brings the opponent into reach. Not at an opponent that is coming in at a run itself: the two would meet with the fighter in the air.

    • counterCrit

      public void counterCrit(boolean on)
      Whether it crits back (COUNTER): with the opponent's sword just spent and its own nearly back, a running jump at an opponent at the edge of the reach and the critical hit on the way down. Players who space it crit it from the edge and sprint-hit it, and before 19 October nothing it did came back at them in their cooldown with a crit. Hit in the air of one, it leaves them alone for a while, as with the chase.

    • onlyAtSpentOrFleeing

      public void onlyAtSpentOrFleeing(boolean on)
      Whether the chase and the hop are made only at an opponent whose sword is spent (OPP_SPENT) or that is running away (FLEEING); see Config.jumpAtReadyOnlyFleeing. An opponent standing its ground with its sword ready hits a running jump out of the air before it comes down.

    • edgeCrit

      public void edgeCrit(boolean on)
      Whether it crits in (EDGE): at an opponent standing still on the ground, a running jump taken from where the way down brings it into reach low in the fall, and the critical hit as it comes into reach; see Config.edgeCritRule. Against an opponent that stands and hits whatever comes into its reach the exchange is otherwise a sprint hit for a hit, 7 for 7 (fight traces, 22 October: 16.6 trades a fight, 0.3 crits); come down into its reach late in a jump and it is a critical hit for a hit, 10.5 for 7. Not near the top of the jump: there the fighter's eye is high above the opponent's head and its reach to it shorter than the opponent's to it, which is how every hop at that opponent was hit out of the air.

    • hopWhy

      For the log: on a tick on the ground with the opponent in view five to PURSUIT_TO blocks off, what kept the last call of plan(float[], int, boolean, boolean, int) from a running jump at it (0: nothing, 1: not at a run yet, 2: hit lately, 3: off to the side, 4: sword not back, 5: left alone after a hit in the air, 6: the opponent coming in fast); -1 on any other tick.

    • distance

      public static float distance(float[] vec)
      How far away the opponent is, read off its height on screen; very far if it is not on screen. What is tall on screen is the side of it that faces the fighter, so this is the distance to its front: a quarter of a block less than to its middle.

    • plan

      public int plan(float[] vec, int keys, boolean onOpponent, boolean busy, int combo)
      One decision.
      Parameters:
      vec - what the network is shown on this tick
      keys - the keys that are the network's on this tick, after the rule about the sword's charge
      onOpponent - whether the game has the opponent under the crosshair and within reach
      busy - the tick is another rule's: it owes the opponent a swing, or is backing out of a combo
      combo - hits it has landed in a row without taking one
      Returns:
      what this tick is to do, as flags; 0 leaves everything to the network
